title: From Cohesion to Norms: How Animal Groups Come, Stay, and Function Together
content:
The present review underscores two salient points: In the context of evolutionary transitions to pair- and group living, it is imperative to acknowledge the distinction between selective forces that act during the origin of these social systems and those that act during their subsequent maintenance. The maintenance of animal groups is contingent upon the presence of cohesion and social order, as these elements are deemed to exert a significant influence on fitness.


ABSTRACT

For over a century, the evolution of social system diversity has been a key focus in the fields of behavior, ecology, evolution, and the social sciences. Unlike many previous studies, which focused on the costs and benefits of evolutionary transitions to pairs or groups, the present paper explores the behavioral mechanisms that mitigate the ensuing costs. Maintaining spatial cohesion is necessary for individuals to reap the benefits of associating with conspecifics. However, this association creates unavoidable costs that promote internal strife and centrifugal forces that drive groups apart. The present review focuses on the behavioral mechanisms that mitigate this trade-off. First, I review features of the three main categories of social systems to identify the emergence and nature of the costs of association. To further differentiate this perspective, I emphasize the importance of distinguishing between the processes that trigger and maintain the evolution of non-solitary systems. In the subsequent section, I summarize the mechanisms by which animal pairs and groups maintain cohesion and social stability. Social order is a foundational concept in the social sciences that describes how unavoidable internal conflict among selfish individuals disrupts social stability. In the final section, I review the factors impacting social order in animals, as well as the fitness consequences of these perturbations, underscoring their evolutionary importance. I argue that behavioral homogeneity among group members serves to enhance social order and can be based on various mechanisms, including social norms. Thus, this broad comparative evaluation offers a novel perspective on the evolutionary roots of a significant component of human social behavior and identifies several novel avenues for future research on the evolution of social systems.
author: Peter M. Kappeler
